l: Jupiter's transformation into a bull, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter lays aside his divine authority and assumes the appearance of a beautiful white bull. The bull has a muscular neck, small transparent horns, and a peaceful, nonthreatening expression.

l: Jupiter's abduction of Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter's abduction begins when Europa sits on the back of the bull without knowing who he is. He gradually enters the water, carries her away from the shore, and takes her across the ocean toward Crete.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains the mythological abduction of Europa, daughter of Agenor, King of Tyre, by Jupiter Asterius. It presents several theories that the story arose from a ship shaped like a bull, a commander named Taurus, or a Phoenician word meaning either ship or bull. Jupiter Asterius is described as the son of Teutamus and as connected with the settlement and first kingship of Crete. After Europa's death, she was honored as a divinity, and a festival called Hellotia was established in her memory.

l: Greek and Roman mythology, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit identifies the story of Europa's abduction as one of the most famous events in ancient Mythology.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The text says that several persons may have borne the name Zeus or Jupiter, making it difficult to assign particular adventures to each one. It attributes various myths to different Jupiters, including the abduction of Ganymede, the deception of Leda, and the abduction of Europa.

l: Jupiter Asterius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter Asterius is identified as the figure associated with the abduction of Europa and is said to have reigned about B.C. 1400. According to the account attributed to Diodorus Siculus, he was the son of Teutamus and was connected with the Pelasgian settlement of Crete, where he was its first king.

l: Crete, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Crete is described as the island where Teutamus and some Pelasgians settled. The text says that it became the kingdom of Jupiter Asterius, who was its first king.

l: Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Europa was the daughter of Agenor, King of Tyre, and was renowned for her beauty. After her death, she was honored as a divinity and received the name Hellotis.

l: Jupiter's abduction of Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The abduction of Europa is explained as a voyage by Jupiter Asterius to carry her away by force. The story may have developed from a ship with a bull-shaped figurehead, a general named Taurus, or the Phoenician word Alpha or Ilpha, which could mean either ship or bull.

l: Hellotia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Hellotia was a festival instituted in memory of Europa after her death. Hesychius connects its name with Hellotis, the name Europa received after death.

l: festival honoring Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: A festival was instituted to honor Europa after her death. Hesychius calls this festival Hellotia.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: Jupiter carries away Europa in the shape of a bull and later reveals himself in the Dictæan land. Agenor commands his son Cadmus to search for Europa, threatening him with exile if he fails to find her. Cadmus consults the oracle of Phœbus, follows a cow to the place where she lies down, and is instructed to build a city there and call the country Bœotia. As Cadmus prepares a sacrifice, his servants approach a spring guarded by a dragon sacred to Mars.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: Jupiter carries away Europa while disguised as a bull, then lays aside that shape and reveals himself in the Dictæan land. His intrigues are unknown to Cadmus, who searches for Europa without knowing what has happened to her.

l: Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: Europa is carried away by Jupiter in the shape of a bull. Her father, Agenor, sends Cadmus to search for her and bring her back.

l: Agenor, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: Agenor commands Cadmus to seek Europa, who has been ravished and carried away. He threatens Cadmus with exile if he does not find her.

l: Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: Cadmus wanders over the whole world while searching for Europa and fleeing his country and his father's wrath. He consults the oracle of Phœbus, follows an unyoked heifer, and reaches the place where she lies down; there he gives thanks, prepares to sacrifice to Jupiter, and sends his servants to fetch water.

l: Delphi, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: Delphi is the place where Cadmus goes to consult the oracle about where he should dwell.

l: the oracle of Delphi, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: The oracle of Phœbus tells Cadmus that an unyoked heifer will meet him and that he must follow her. It instructs him to build a city where the heifer lies down and to call the country Bœotia.

l: Phœbus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: Phœbus, through his oracle, directs Cadmus to follow an unyoked heifer and establish a city where she rests. Cadmus silently worships Phœbus as the adviser of his way.

l: heifer, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: The heifer has never borne the yoke and shows no mark of servitude on her neck. She leads Cadmus through the fields, stops after crossing the Cephisus and the fields of Panope, and lies down on the grass.

l: Bœotia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: Bœotia is the name that Phœbus's oracle instructs Cadmus to give to the country where the heifer lies down.

l: Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: Cadmus is instructed to build the city at the place where the heifer lies down. The city has not yet been built in this unit.

l: dragon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE THIRD.
s: The dragon is sacred to Mars and hides in a cavern within an ancient grove. It has crests, a golden color, fiery eyes, a body swollen with poison, three tongues, and teeth arranged in three rows.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The notes explain that Cadmus continued his search after Telephassa’s death and went to Delphi to consult the oracle. They describe Europa’s ancestry according to Apollodorus: Libya and Neptune had Belus and Agenor, and Agenor and Telephassa had Cadmus, Phœnix, Cilix, and Europa. Other writers instead made Europa the daughter of Phœnix and granddaughter of Agenor. The explanation also discusses theories that Europe was named after Europa or after the fair complexion of its inhabitants.

l: Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: According to Apollodorus, Cadmus lived in Thrace until the death of his mother, Telephassa, and then went to Delphi to consult the oracle. He was the son of Agenor and Telephassa.

l: Telephassa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Telephassa accompanied Cadmus while he lived in Thrace and died before he proceeded to Delphi. She was the wife of Agenor and the mother of Cadmus, Phœnix, Cilix, and Europa according to Apollodorus.

l: Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: According to Apollodorus, Europa was the daughter of Agenor and Telephassa and the sister of Cadmus, Phœnix, and Cilix. Some ancient writers instead described her as the daughter of Phœnix and granddaughter of Agenor; she may have received her name from her fair complexion.

l: Agenor, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Agenor was the son of Libya and Neptune, according to Apollodorus. He married Telephassa and had Cadmus, Phœnix, Cilix, and Europa.

l: Europe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Some authors, including Ovid, supposed that Europe received its name from Europa. Bochart suggested that the name originally referred to the fair complexion of the people who inhabited it.

l: genealogy of Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: According to Apollodorus, Libya had two sons by Neptune, Belus and Agenor; Agenor married Telephassa, and their children were Cadmus, Phœnix, Cilix, and Europa. Other writers made Europa the daughter of Phœnix and the granddaughter of Agenor.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cadmus's companions go to the fountain of Mars for water and are devoured by the dragon guarding it. Cadmus finds their bodies, fights the dragon, and kills it by pinning its throat to an oak with his spear. At Minerva's advice, Cadmus sows the dragon's teeth, from which armed earth-born warriors arise and kill one another until five remain. These five assist Cadmus in building the city of Thebes, as ordered by the oracle of Phœbus.

l: Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cadmus, the son of Agenor, discovers that his companions have been destroyed and vows either to avenge their deaths or share them. He fights and kills the dragon, then follows Minerva's advice by sowing its teeth; after the earth-born warriors destroy one another, the five survivors assist him in building the city of Thebes.

l: Cadmus's companions, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cadmus's companions, men from the Tyrian nation, go to the fountain of Mars to fetch water. The dragon attacks and devours them, killing some with its sting, some with its coils, and some with its poisonous breath.

l: dragon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The dragon guarding the fountain of Mars emerges from its cave when Cadmus's companions disturb the grove. It attacks them, battles Cadmus, and is finally killed when Cadmus drives his spear through its throat and into an oak.

l: fountain of Mars, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The fountain of Mars is the place where Cadmus's companions go to draw water. The dragon guarding it emerges from a deep cave when their urns enter the water.

l: the grove, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The grove is entered by the men from the Tyrian nation, who disturb the water while fetching it. Cadmus later enters the grove and finds his companions dead and the victorious dragon upon them.

l: Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Minerva, the favorer of Cadmus, descends through the air and tells him to sow the dragon's teeth under the earth as seeds of a future people. Her advice leads to the arising of the armed earth-born warriors.

l: the dragon's teeth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: At Minerva's direction, Cadmus scatters the dragon's teeth in furrows under the earth. They produce armed men, who emerge first with spears and helmets and then with shields and other weapons.

l: the earth-born warriors, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The earth-born warriors arise from the dragon's teeth as a crop of armed men. They become maddened and kill one another in civil war, leaving only five survivors.

l: the five surviving earth-born warriors, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Five of the earth-born warriors survive the fighting, and Echion is one of them. At the advice of Minerva, he throws down his arms and exchanges assurances of brotherly concord with the others; the five then assist Cadmus in building the city.

l: the dragon's death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The dragon's death comes after Cadmus wounds it with his spear and pursues it as it retreats. He presses the spear through its throat until the dragon's neck is pierced together with the trunk of an oak.

l: the dragon's sowing, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cadmus performs the dragon's sowing by opening a furrow with a plough and scattering the dragon's teeth on the ground. The teeth immediately produce armed earth-born warriors.

l: the earth-born warriors' civil war, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The earth-born warriors' civil war begins when one of them strikes a brother with a sword after telling Cadmus not to engage in civil war. The warriors then kill one another with swords and darts until only five remain.

l: Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Thebes is the city that Cadmus builds with the assistance of the five surviving earth-born warriors. Its construction is undertaken as ordered by the oracle of Phœbus.

l: the building of Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The building of Thebes is carried out by Cadmus with the five surviving earth-born warriors as his associates. The city is built according to the order of the oracle of Phœbus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains the notes on the dragon encountered by Cadmus and the myth of the earth-born warriors. Agenor sent his sons to search for his lost daughter, while Cadmus eventually settled in Bœotia, killed the dragon, and sowed its teeth. The explanation presents alternative interpretations in which the dragon was a hostile king or serpent and the dragon’s teeth and earth-born men represented soldiers who joined Cadmus. These men helped Cadmus defeat his enemies and build the citadel of Thebes, while Apollodorus says that Cadmus served Mars to atone for killing the dragon.

l: Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Cadmus was sent by Agenor to search for his lost sister but did not return, eventually settling in Bœotia. He killed the dragon, sowed its teeth, and was said to receive assistance from men who sprang from the earth; these men helped him defeat his enemies and build the citadel of Thebes. Apollodorus says that Cadmus served Mars for a year to expiate the dragon’s slaughter.

l: Agenor, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Agenor commanded his sons to search for his lost daughter and not to return until they had found her. His sons failed to bring her back and established themselves in different countries.

l: dragon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The dragon slain by Cadmus was described in the notes as enormous and capable of killing prey by its sting, coils, or poisonous breath. Other writers identified it as a king named Draco, a son of Mars, while Heraclitus maintained that Cadmus really killed a serpent that troubled Bœotia.

l: Mars, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Mars was identified as the father of the dragon in one interpretation of the myth. According to Apollodorus, Cadmus served Mars for a year as punishment for killing the dragon.

l: the dragon's teeth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The dragon’s teeth were sown by Cadmus and were said to produce armed men. The explanation proposes that they symbolized soldiers or short brass-pointed javelins because related words in the Phoenician language could have both meanings.

l: the earth-born warriors, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The earth-born men were said to emerge after Cadmus sowed the dragon’s teeth. The explanation interprets them as local people or soldiers whom Cadmus won to his side; they helped him conquer his enemies and build the citadel of Thebes.

l: Bœotia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Bœotia was the region where Cadmus settled. The dragon slain by Cadmus was also described as a serpent that greatly troubled the Bœotian territory.

l: Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Thebes received its citadel when the men associated with the dragon’s teeth helped Cadmus defeat his enemies and construct a fortified settlement.

l: Cadmus's soldiers, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Cadmus’s soldiers are presented in the explanation as the men symbolized by the dragon’s teeth and the earth-born warriors. They were armed with helmets, body armor, and brass-pointed darts, and assisted Cadmus in conquering his enemies and establishing Thebes.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Actæon, grandson of Cadmus, accidentally enters Gargaphie and sees Diana bathing with her Nymphs. Diana transforms him into a stag after he sees her without her garments. Actæon's hunting dogs pursue and tear apart their own master, while his companions unknowingly urge them on. The text presents Actæon's misfortune as an accident rather than a crime.

l: Actæon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Actæon, the grandson of Cadmus and a skilled hunter, enters the Gargaphie grove after postponing the remainder of his hunt. He accidentally sees Diana bathing, is transformed into a stag, and is pursued and torn apart by his own dogs.

l: Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cadmus is described as having reached great prosperity in Thebes through his illustrious wife, children, and grandchildren. Actæon's transformation and death become the first major sorrow among his many blessings.

l: Diana, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Diana, goddess of the woods and of the hunt, bathes in the usual retreat of Gargaphie with her Nymphs. After Actæon sees her without her garments, she sprinkles him with water, transforms him into a stag, and is said not to be satisfied until his many wounds end his life.

l: Diana's Nymphs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Diana's Nymphs assist her while she bathes: they carry her hunting equipment, remove her sandals and mantle, arrange her hair, and fetch and pour water. When Actæon enters, they shriek, strike their breasts, and surround Diana to cover her bodies.

l: Gargaphie, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Gargaphie is a valley thickly planted with pitch-trees and cypress, sacred to the active Diana. Its secluded recess contains a natural grotto and a clear fountain where Diana bathes after hunting.

l: Actæon’s dogs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Actæon's numerous hunting dogs pursue him after he has been transformed into a stag. They wound and tear apart their master, failing to recognize him, while his companions urge them on and call aloud for Actæon.

l: Actæon’s transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Diana's avenging water gives Actæon the horns, neck, ears, feet, legs, and spotted coat of a lively stag, and fear is added to his condition. His former understanding remains, but he can no longer speak as a man.

l: Actæon’s death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Actæon dies after his own dogs surround him and bury their jaws in his body. His companions do not understand what is happening and continue to seek Actæon as though he were absent.

l: Diana bathing, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Actæon enters the unknown wood with uncertain steps and inadvertently reaches Diana's bathing place. The text states that his fault is accidental rather than criminal, because his sight of Diana without her garments results from mistaken wandering.

l: hunting, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Actæon and his companions hunt through a mountain marked by the blood of wild beasts. After the day's sport, Actæon orders the men to stop, remove the nets, and resume the hunt on the following morning.

l: Gargaphie grotto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Gargaphie grotto lies in the secluded part of a grove and is formed naturally from pumice and light sand-stone in an arch-like shape. A clear fountain runs beside it, and Diana uses the grotto as a bathing place after hunting.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit provides notes and explanations about the fable of Actæon, who saw Diana bathing and was punished. It identifies Actæon as a Boeotian youth and lists the names and meanings of many of his hunting dogs. The explanation criticizes Ovid’s portrayal of Diana’s cruel revenge and discusses several ancient interpretations of Actæon’s transformation and death. Some sources say that Actæon’s dogs devoured him, while others explain the story symbolically or assign different offenses to him.

l: Actæon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Actæon is identified as the son of Autonoë and Aristæus and as a Boeotian youth, called Hyantian because the Hyantes were the ancient inhabitants of Boeotia. He was brought up by Chiron according to Apollodorus, and ancient accounts variously say that he was punished for seeing Diana bathing, showing contempt for Diana, attempting improper advances toward Semele, or approaching Diana out of curiosity.

l: Diana, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Diana is described in the explanation as chaste and prudent, though Ovid portrays her as taking cruel revenge on Actæon for seeing her bathing. The text discusses several Dianas and suggests that this episode most probably belongs to Diana Britomartis, who was particularly fond of the chase.

l: Actæon’s transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Actæon’s transformation is treated as a punishment inflicted by Diana after he saw her bathing. The explanation notes alternative interpretations in which Actæon was not literally transformed, but was said to have been devoured by his dogs after they became mad or after his hunting establishment ruined him.

l: Actæon’s death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Actæon’s death is variously attributed to his own hunting dogs, which some authors say became mad and devoured him. Apollodorus places his death on Mount Cithæron after he saw Diana bathing, while other ancient authorities connect it with his contempt for Diana or his advances toward Semele.

l: Actæon’s dogs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Actæon’s pack is said to have consisted of fifty dogs, although Ovid names thirty-six and other writers preserve different lists. Their names often describe their qualities or origins, such as Melampus ('Black-foot'), Ichnobates ('Tracer'), Pamphagus ('Glutton'), and Lælaps ('Tempest'); Apollodorus says that the dogs died of grief after losing their master.

l: Diana bathing, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Diana was bathing at the time Actæon saw her. Pausanias says that Actæon’s curiosity was aroused by the novelty of the sight and led him to approach nearer.

l: Actæon fable, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The fable presents Diana as punishing Actæon for the misfortune or indiscretion of seeing her naked. Ancient accounts differ about the cause and meaning of the story, including literal transformation and death by his dogs, a symbolic account of financial ruin from maintaining hounds, and claims that Actæon had offended Diana or pursued Semele.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Juno, enraged that Semele is pregnant by Jupiter, resolves to destroy her and transfers her hatred of Jupiter's Tyrian mistress to Semele. Disguised as the old nurse Beroë, Juno persuades Semele to demand that Jupiter appear in the same divine splendor in which he approaches Juno. Semele asks Jupiter to grant this request, and he swears by the Styx that he will deny her nothing. Regretting the oath, Jupiter prepares to appear with clouds, storms, lightning, thunder, and the thunderbolt.

l: Juno, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Juno rejoices at Semele's pregnancy by Jupiter and resolves to destroy her. She disguises herself as Beroë and persuades Semele to test Jupiter by demanding that he appear in his full divine majesty.

l: Semele, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Semele is pregnant by Jupiter and accepts Juno's deceptive advice while disguised as Beroë. She asks Jupiter to appear to her in the form in which he is received by Juno.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter promises Semele that she may choose any favor and swears that he will not deny it. After she makes her request, he regrets having sworn but prepares to approach with clouds, winds, rain, lightning, thunder, and the thunderbolt.

l: Beroë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Beroë is identified as the Epidaurian nurse of Semele. Juno assumes Beroë's form and uses the disguise to deceive Semele.

l: the pregnancy of Semele, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Semele's pregnancy by Jupiter intensifies Juno's anger. Juno views it as evidence of Jupiter's crime and resents that Semele is about to become a mother by him.

l: Juno's revenge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Juno's revenge consists of deceiving Semele into asking Jupiter to appear in his full divine splendor. She intends for Semele to be destroyed by the consequences of that request.

l: Jupiter's oath, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter's oath is sworn by the Styx, which he calls the dread stream and the God of the Gods. Because he has sworn to grant Semele whatever she chooses, he cannot withdraw from her request.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Fable most probably arose from an intrigue between Semele and one of the princes called Jupiter, which ended tragically. Pausanias says that Cadmus had Semele and her son thrown into the sea, after which Semele reached Oreate and was buried there. According to Apollodorus, Bacchus later brought Semele from hell and carried her to heaven, where she was ranked among the Goddesses as Thyone. Nonnus describes her as conversing with Pallas and Diana and dining with Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, and Venus.

l: Semele, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Semele was involved in an intrigue with one of the princes called Jupiter, which ended tragically. Cadmus caused her and her son to be thrown into the sea; she came ashore at Oreate and was buried there. After her death, she was ranked among the Goddesses as Thyone, and Bacchus brought her from hell to heaven.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter was one of the princes associated with the intrigue involving Semele. After Semele was taken to heaven, she ate at the same table as Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, and Venus.

l: Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Bacchus was the son of Semele. He went down to hell, brought Semele from there, and carried her up to heaven.

l: Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: According to Pausanias, Cadmus was exasperated against his daughter Semele and caused her and her son to be thrown into the sea.

l: intrigue between Semele and Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The intrigue between Semele and one of the princes called Jupiter is presented as the probable historical event that gave occasion to the Fable. It ended tragically.

l: death of Semele and her son, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Pausanias says that Semele and her son were thrown into the sea by Cadmus. They were cast ashore at Oreate, where Semele was buried.

l: Fable, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Fable most probably arose from a tragic intrigue between Semele and one of the princes called Jupiter. Its later account includes Semele's elevation among the Goddesses after Bacchus brought her from hell to heaven.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter visits Semele as promised, but the effulgence of his lightning burns her to ashes. Bacchus, whom Semele is carrying, is removed from her womb and placed in Jupiter's thigh until he completes his gestation, after which Ino and the Nyseian Nymphs care for him. Jupiter and Juno dispute whether sexual pleasure is greater for females or males, and Tiresias confirms Jupiter's opinion after having experienced both sexes. Juno punishes Tiresias by making him permanently blind, while Jupiter grants him knowledge of future events.

l: Semele, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Semele is visited by Jupiter according to the promise he had made. Her mortal body cannot endure the force of his divine lightning, and she is burned to ashes among her nuptial presents.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter visits Semele while using a less destructive form of thunder, but its divine force still burns her. Later, after drinking nectar, he disputes with Juno about whether females or males experience greater sexual pleasure, and he grants Tiresias knowledge of future events after Juno blinds him.

l: Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Bacchus is preserved even though Semele is burned while pregnant with him. Ino secretly nurses him at first, and the Nyseian Nymphs later hide him in their caves and feed him milk.

l: Juno, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Juno disputes Jupiter's claim that females experience greater sexual pleasure than males. After Tiresias confirms Jupiter's opinion, she grieves excessively and condemns Tiresias to eternal blindness.

l: Tiresias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Tiresias becomes a woman after striking two coupling serpents with his staff and remains female for seven autumns. After striking the same serpents again in the eighth year, he regains his former sex and shape. Because he has experienced both forms of pleasure, he is chosen to judge the dispute between Jupiter and Juno.

l: Semele's burning, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Semele's mortal body is unable to withstand Jupiter's divine lightning, and she is burned to ashes in his presence.

l: Bacchus's premature birth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The infant Bacchus is removed from Semele's womb before he is fully formed. He is inserted into Jupiter's thigh and completes there the time he would otherwise have spent in the womb.

l: Tiresias's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Tiresias changes from a man into a woman after striking two serpents that are coupling in a green wood. Seven years later, he strikes the serpents again and returns to his original sex and shape.

l: dispute over sexual pleasure, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter claims that females receive greater sexual pleasure than males, while Juno denies it. Tiresias, who has experienced both sexes, is asked to decide the dispute and confirms Jupiter's claim.

l: Tiresias's blindness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Tiresias is condemned to eternal darkness after confirming Jupiter's opinion in the dispute over sexual pleasure. Jupiter later compensates him by granting knowledge of things to come.

l: Juno's punishment of Tiresias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Juno punishes Tiresias for confirming Jupiter's claim by condemning his eyes to eternal darkness. Jupiter cannot reverse the act of another deity, so he alleviates the punishment by giving Tiresias prophetic knowledge.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: The unit explains that the Nyseian Nymphs brought up Bacchus in Nysa, where he was concealed from the fury of Juno. It names the nymphs as Cysseis, Nysa, Erato, Eryphia, Bromia, and Polyhymnia. The cave where Bacchus was concealed was said to have two entrances, and the name Nysa contributed in part to his Greek name Dionysus.

l: Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: Bacchus was brought up by the Nyseian Nymphs in Nysa and concealed in a cave from the fury of Juno. Because the cave was said to have two entrances, he received the epithet Dithyrites; the name Nysa also contributed in part to his Greek name Dionysus.

l: Nyseian Nymphs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: The Nyseian Nymphs brought up Bacchus in Nysa. They were named Cysseis, Nysa, Erato, Eryphia, Bromia, and Polyhymnia.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Narcissus, son of Cephisus and Liriope, is renowned for his beauty and rejects everyone who courts him. A prophecy says he will live to old age only if he never recognizes himself. Juno punishes Echo by limiting her speech because Echo distracted her with stories while Jupiter's mistresses escaped. Echo falls in love with Narcissus, but he rejects her, and she wastes away until only her voice remains.

l: Echo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Echo was once a noisy Nymph who distracted Juno with long stories so Jupiter's mistresses could escape. Juno punished her by allowing her only to repeat the last words spoken by others. After Narcissus rejected her, Echo hid in the woods, wasted away, and was never seen again, though she continued to be heard.

l: Juno, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Juno was repeatedly detained by Echo's stories while Jupiter's mistresses escaped. When Juno discovered the deception, she punished Echo by limiting her use of speech.

l: Narcissus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Narcissus was the beautiful son of Cephisus and Liriope, celebrated throughout the cities of Aonia for his beauty. Many youths and damsels courted him, but he rejected them all. He rejected Echo when she tried to embrace him.

l: the prophecy about Narcissus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The prophet said that Narcissus would see mature old age only if he never recognized himself. The prophecy initially seemed frivolous, but the manner of his death and the unusual nature of his frenzy later confirmed it.

l: Echo's love for Narcissus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Echo fell in love with Narcissus after seeing him drive timid stags into his nets. Her love grew stronger as she followed him and suffered his refusal. After he rejected her, she remained hidden in the woods, while her love continued.

l: Echo's voice, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Echo's voice could repeat the last words spoken by others, and she used it to answer Narcissus when he called out. After her body wasted away and her bones became stones, her voice alone remained alive and continued to be heard in the mountains and woods.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The notes explain the names Aonia, Liriope, and Narcissus, and comment on ancient customs involving sulphur-tipped torches. The explanation treats the story of Echo as an attempt to account for an extraordinary natural phenomenon through natural philosophy rather than history. It says that the poets portrayed Echo as the daughter of the Air and the Tongue and Pan as in love with her. Historically, the story may have originated with a Nymph lost in the woods, whose rescuers heard only echoes of their own voices.

l: Narcissus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Narcissus was the son of Liriope and the river Cephisus. His name is derived from the Greek word ναρκᾷν, meaning “to fade away,” which characterized his career and the duration of the flower.

l: Echo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The poets represented Echo as the daughter of the Air and the Tongue. The explanation suggests that the story may have arisen from a Nymph who became lost in the woods, while those searching for her heard only echoes of their own voices.

l: Pan, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The poets said that Pan fell in love with Echo. The explanation suggests that someone represented under the name of Pan may have tried to discover the cause of the extraordinary phenomenon.

l: extraordinary phenomenon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The extraordinary phenomenon is the echo, understood as the sound of people’s own voices returning to them. The poets may have invented the fable to explain this phenomenon.

l: fable, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The fable concerns Echo and Pan and was probably invented to explain an extraordinary phenomenon. Its embellishments include making Echo the daughter of the Air and the Tongue and saying that Pan loved her.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Narcissus, having rejected many Nymphs and youths, is cursed to love without possessing what he loves. At a clear, untouched spring, he falls in love with his own reflection and wastes away while gazing at it. Echo repeats his words and laments his decline. After Narcissus dies, his body disappears and a yellow flower with white leaves is found in its place.

l: Narcissus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Narcissus goes to a clear spring after hunting and becomes captivated by his own reflection. He neglects food and rest, wastes away from love, and dies after bidding farewell to the image.

l: Echo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Echo repeats Narcissus's cries, words, and sounds. Although she is angry and remembers how he treated her, she grieves as he wastes away and laments his death.

l: the Gods, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Gods change Narcissus into a flower after his death. Rhamnusia assents to the prayer that he should love without enjoying what he loves.

l: the clear spring, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The clear spring has unsullied, silver-like water untouched by shepherds, animals, birds, or falling branches. Grass and a surrounding wood shade it from the sun, and its water reflects Narcissus's form.

l: Narcissus's reflection, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Narcissus's reflection appears to him as a beautiful body, although it has no substance and is only a shadow. It mirrors his gestures, smiles, tears, and words, but disappears or becomes distorted when the water is disturbed.

l: Narcissus flower, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: After Narcissus's body cannot be found, a yellow flower with white leaves surrounding its middle is discovered in its place. The flower bears his name.

l: Narcissus's love, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Narcissus's love is directed toward his own reflection, which he does not recognize as himself at first. It gives him pleasure and torment, consumes his strength, and leaves him wishing that what he loves could live longer.

l: Narcissus's death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Narcissus's death follows his prolonged wasting from love and ends his sorrows. His Naiad sisters and the Dryads mourn him, while Echo resounds with their lamentations.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains that Narcissus was a Thespian whose story serves as a moral lesson about the fatal effects of self-love. His pursuit of his own image is compared to the unreal pleasures that people eagerly pursue. Pausanias gives a different account in which Narcissus mistakes his reflection for the shade of his dead sister and dies of grief. The unit also discusses Tiresias, the renowned soothsayer who predicted Narcissus’s fate and became blind late in life.

l: Narcissus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Narcissus was a Thespian by birth. In Pausanias’s version, he loved his sister, who resembled him and accompanied him in the chase; after her death, he mistook his reflection in a fountain for her shade, pined away, and died of grief.

l: Narcissus's story, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The story is presented as a moral lesson revealing the fatal effects of self-love. Its account of Narcissus pursuing an image that continually withdraws from his embrace is compared to the limited reality found in many pleasures that people eagerly pursue.

l: self-love, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Self-love is portrayed as having potentially fatal effects, as illustrated by Narcissus’s pursuit of his own image.

l: Pausanias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Pausanias gives a different version of Narcissus’s story in his Bœotica. He places the fountain near Donacon, in the country of the Thespians, and regards Narcissus’s transformation into a flower as a fiction.

l: Tiresias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Tiresias predicted Narcissus’s untoward fate and was the son of Evenus and Chariclo. He was regarded as the most renowned soothsayer of his time, lived to a great age, and became blind toward the end of his life; different accounts attribute his death or blindness to drinking from a fountain, seeing Minerva bathing, or his teachings about the sexes of animals and stars.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Tiresias predicts that Pentheus will be torn apart if he refuses to honor Bacchus, whose arrival in Greece is accompanied by public celebrations. Pentheus rejects the prophecy, forbids Bacchic worship, and orders Bacchus captured, but Bacchus’s follower Acœtes recounts how the god transformed impious sailors into dolphins. Pentheus then goes to Mount Cithæron to stop the rites, where Agave and the other Bacchantes attack and dismember him. Afterward, the matrons of Thebes accept the new worship and honor Bacchus’s altars.

l: Pentheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pentheus, son of Echion, ridicules Tiresias and refuses to honor Bacchus. He orders Bacchus to be captured, rejects Acœtes’s account of the god’s power, and goes to Mount Cithæron to disrupt the rites. There, his mother Agave and the other Bacchantes attack and tear him apart.

l: Tiresias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Tiresias is praised throughout the cities of Achaia for his prophetic powers, but Pentheus mocks him for his blindness. He predicts that Pentheus will be torn apart and that his blood will pollute the woods, his mother, and his mother’s sisters if Pentheus refuses to honor Bacchus.

l: Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Bacchus arrives in Greece as the new god Liber, and festive howlings announce his worship. After sailors attempt to deceive and transport him, he stops their ship, causes vines and wild creatures to appear, and transforms the crew into dolphin-like creatures, while Acœtes is spared. His sacred rites continue on Mount Cithæron.

l: Acœtes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Acœtes, an Etrurian sailor and follower of Bacchus, is captured and brought before Pentheus. He tells how Bacchus was taken aboard his ship and how the god punished the sailors who tried to deceive him. Pentheus orders Acœtes tortured, but the prison doors open and his chains fall away by themselves.

l: Agave, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Agave, Pentheus’s mother, is among the Bacchantes on Mount Cithæron. In her frenzy she strikes Pentheus, helps tear him apart, and holds up his severed head while claiming victory.

l: Bacchantes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Bacchantes celebrate the rites of Bacchus on Mount Cithæron. When Pentheus appears and watches with profane eyes, they pursue and attack him, tearing his body apart.

l: Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pentheus fears that Thebes will be captured by Bacchus, whom he describes as an unarmed and effeminate boy. After Pentheus’s death, the Ismenian matrons of Thebes adopt the new worship, burn incense, and honor the sacred altars.

l: Mount Cithæron, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Mount Cithæron is the place chosen for the celebration of Bacchic rites and resounds with singing and the cries of Bacchus’s worshippers. Pentheus goes there to interrupt the ceremonies and is dismembered in its woods.

l: Bacchus festivals, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Bacchic rites spread through Greece with festive howlings and attract matrons, newly married women, men, and people of every rank. They are celebrated on Mount Cithæron, where Pentheus’s intrusion leads to his destruction.

l: Pentheus’s dismemberment, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pentheus’s dismemberment fulfills Tiresias’s prophecy. Agave first wounds him, Autonoë and Ino tear away his arms, and Agave and the other Bacchantes rip his body apart and remove his head.

l: Tiresias’s prophecy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Tiresias prophesies that Pentheus will be scattered and torn apart if he refuses to honor Bacchus. The prophecy is fulfilled when Pentheus is dismembered by his mother and the other Bacchantes on Mount Cithæron.

l: Bacchus’s arrival in Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Bacchus enters Greece in triumph as the new god Liber, and his arrival is marked by public processions, music, dancing, and unfamiliar rites. Pentheus attempts to suppress his worship, but Bacchus’s rites prevail and are eventually honored by the matrons of Thebes.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains references connected with Bacchus, including his symbols, festivals, worship, and the story of Pentheus. Pentheus, king of Thebes and grandson of Cadmus, opposed the abuses associated with Bacchic worship and was torn apart by Bacchantes, including his mother Agave. The account also describes Bacchus’s punishment of impious mariners near Naxos and discusses traditions identifying Bacchus with the Egyptian Osiris. It further explains the Trieterica and the role of Cithæron in Bacchic rites.

l: Pentheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Pentheus was the son of Echion and Agave, grandson of Cadmus, and king of Thebes after succeeding his grandfather. He opposed abuses in the mysteries of Bacchus and went to Cithæron to chastise the Bacchantes, who tore him to pieces in their frenzy. Another account says that he was a wicked prince who climbed a tree to observe the secret rites and was killed after the Bacchantes discovered him.

l: Agave, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Agave was the daughter of Cadmus and the mother of Pentheus. She was among the Bacchantes who, in their frantic madness, tore Pentheus apart.

l: Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Cadmus was the father of Agave and the grandfather of Pentheus. The account says that Bacchus’s mysteries were dedicated to Bacchus in gratitude to the family of Cadmus for favors received.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter was said to be the father of several accounts of Bacchus, including the Theban Bacchus, whose mother was Semele. One explanation of Bacchus’s birth says that Jupiter carried him in his thigh, a story possibly based on a Greek word that can also mean the hollow of a mountain.

l: Naxos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Naxos was the most famous island of the Cyclades and was sacred to Bacchus. The mariners in the account were probably shipwrecked near Naxos, and their transformation was associated with their possible neglect or contempt of Bacchus’s mysteries.

l: Mount Cithæron, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Cithæron was a mountain of Bœotia famous for the orgies of Bacchus. Pentheus went there to chastise the Bacchantes who were celebrating the festival.

l: Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Bacchus is described as a deity associated with the vine, thyrsi, tambourines, ivy, and ecstatic worship. He was said to have taught useful arts, gained the esteem of neighboring countries, and spread his worship widely. The account also says that he punished impious mariners by transforming them, while some traditions identify the ancient Bacchus with Osiris.

l: Trieterica, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Trieterica was a festival celebrated every three years in honor of Bacchus. During it, Bacchantes carried the figure of the god in a chariot drawn by tigers or panthers, ran around it with thyrsi, and shouted his names while playing tambourines and brazen instruments.

l: Osiris, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Osiris is identified by Herodotus and Plutarch as the true and most ancient Bacchus. His worship was said to have passed from Egypt to Greece, where it underwent alterations and was connected with the mysteries later dedicated to Bacchus.

l: Semele, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Semele was the mother of the Theban Bacchus and was said to have delivered him in the seventh month. The shortened gestation was used to explain the story that Jupiter carried Bacchus in his thigh for the remaining period.

l: Bacchus's worship, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Bacchic worship included mysteries, ecstatic rites, thyrsi, tambourines, vine and ivy imagery, and cries such as “Evoë. Bacche!” Greek additions to the Egyptian-derived ceremonial were described as involving licentious practices and serious offenses, which were repeatedly suppressed and re-established.

l: Bacchantes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Bacchantes were worshippers of Bacchus who celebrated his rites with frantic movements, thyrsi, vine leaves, tambourines, and brazen instruments. At Cithæron, they tore Pentheus apart; among them were his mother Agave and his aunt.

l: Bacchus festivals, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Bacchus festivals included the Trieterica and rites held on Cithæron. Participants carried the god’s image, wore vine leaves, bore thyrsi, used musical instruments, and called Bacchus by names including Bromius, Lyæus, Evan, Lenæus, and Sabazius.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Alcithoë and the other daughters of Minyas reject the rites of Bacchus and remain indoors working while the Bacchic festival proceeds. One daughter tells how Pyramus and Thisbe, lovers in Babylon whose parents forbid their marriage, arrange to meet at the tomb of Ninus. Thisbe flees from a lioness and leaves behind her veil, leading Pyramus to believe she has died and to kill himself with his sword. Thisbe returns, finds Pyramus dead, and kills herself with the same sword; their bodies are placed in one urn, and the mulberry fruit becomes dark.

l: Alcithoë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Alcithoë, daughter of Minyas, rejects the rites of Bacchus and rashly denies that Bacchus is the progeny of Jupiter. She joins her sisters in this impiety.

l: three daughters of Minyas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: The daughters of Minyas refuse to celebrate the festival of Bacchus and remain indoors, carding wool, spinning thread, weaving, and directing their handmaids. They pass the time by telling stories, including the story of Pyramus and Thisbe.

l: Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Bacchus is invoked under many names during the festival, including Bromius, Lyæus, Nyseus, Thyoneus, Lenæus, Nyctelius, Eleleus, Iacchus, and Evan. He is described as eternally youthful, a conqueror of the East, and the destroyer of Pentheus and Lycurgus.

l: Bacchus festivals, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: The priest orders matrons, maids, and new-married women to wear skins, loosen their hair, crown themselves, carry green thyrsi, offer frankincense, and invoke Bacchus. The festival includes Bacchanals, Satyrs, Silenus, shouts, tambourines, cymbals, and pipes, while the Ismenian matrons celebrate the sacred rites.

l: Pyramus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Pyramus is described as the most beautiful of youths and as the lover of Thisbe. Believing that Thisbe has been killed, he mourns her, wounds himself with his sword, and dies beneath the agreed-upon tree.

l: Thisbe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Thisbe is described as the most favored of the damsels of the East and as Pyramus's beloved. She reaches the meeting place first, flees from a lioness, returns after Pyramus has killed himself, and then kills herself.

l: Babylon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Babylon is the city where Pyramus and Thisbe live in adjoining houses. It is said to have been surrounded by the lofty brick walls of Semiramis.

l: lovers' meeting, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Pyramus and Thisbe arrange to meet at night outside the city, at the tomb of Ninus beneath a mulberry tree. Thisbe arrives first, but the meeting is disrupted when she flees from a lioness.

l: tomb of Ninus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: The tomb of Ninus is the agreed meeting place of Pyramus and Thisbe. It stands beneath the shade of a lofty mulberry tree near a cold spring.

l: mulberry tree, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: The mulberry tree near the tomb of Ninus initially bears snow-white fruit. After Pyramus's blood reaches it, the tree's fruit becomes dark or purple, and it later shades the bodies of both lovers.

l: lioness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: A lioness with jaws stained by the recent slaughter of oxen comes to the spring to drink. It tears Thisbe's veil after Thisbe has fled into a dark cave.

l: Thisbe's veil, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Thisbe drops her veil while fleeing from the lioness. The lioness tears it and stains it with blood, and Pyramus later finds it and mistakes it for evidence that Thisbe has been killed.

l: Pyramus's sword, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Pyramus uses the sword with which he is girt to plunge into his bowels. After he draws it from the wound, Thisbe uses the same bloodied sword to kill herself.

l: Pyramus and Thisbe's love, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Pyramus and Thisbe live in adjoining houses and fall deeply in love, though their fathers forbid their marriage. They communicate through a small crack in the party-wall and arrange to meet secretly outside the city.

l: Pyramus's suicide, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Pyramus believes that the bloodied veil proves Thisbe has died and blames himself for her supposed death. He kisses the veil, wounds himself with his sword, and dies beneath the mulberry tree.

l: Thisbe's suicide, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Thisbe finds Pyramus dying beneath the mulberry tree and declares that love and her own hand will give her strength to follow him. She plunges into the sword that is still reeking with Pyramus's blood.

l: Pyramus and Thisbe's deaths and burial, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: Pyramus dies after stabbing himself, and Thisbe dies by the same sword after finding him. Their prayers move the gods and their parents, and what remains of them after the funeral pyre is placed in the same urn.

l: mulberry fruit's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FOURTH.
s: The mulberry fruit is changed by Pyramus's blood from white to a dark or purple color. It remains black when fully ripe as a memorial to the blood and fate of both lovers.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains notes concerning Alcithoë, the daughters of Minyas, and the worship and rites of Bacchus, including the meanings of several names and the opposition to his cult. It discusses Dercetis, her association with fish imagery, Semiramis, and Babylon. It also explains the story of Pyramus and Thisbe, whose meeting and deaths are associated with Babylon, and interprets the tale as a moral story. The unit compares this story with Shakspere’s Midsummer Night’s Dream.

l: Alcithoë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Alcithoë was the daughter of Minyas and one of the women who refused to join the rites of Bacchus. She is associated with the story in which the daughters of Minyas were said to have been changed into bats.

l: Minyas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Minyas was said to be the son of Orchomenus, or, according to another account, the father of Orchomenus. Pausanias says that the Bœotians were called Minyæ after him.

l: Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Bacchus was worshipped through the Dionysia and various rites, which met with opposition in Greece. He was known by names including Bromius, Lyæus, Thyoneus, Lenæus, Nyctelius, Eleleus, Iacchus, and Evan, and was said to have punished those who neglected his worship.

l: festival of Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Dionysia was originally called orgia and was a festival of Bacchus. Over time, the word orgia came to refer to any occasion of festivity.

l: Dercetis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Dercetis, also called Derceto or Atergatis, was represented in some accounts as a woman from the waist upward and a fish below. She was said to have drowned herself near Ascalon and to have been changed into a fish, and she was worshipped by the Syrians.

l: Semiramis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Semiramis was said to have consecrated a temple near Hieropolis to her mother, Dercetis, rather than to Juno. She was also said to have built the brick walls of Babylon, and Dercetis was reported to have been her mother.

l: Babylon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Babylon was described as a lofty and magnificent city with extensive walls built of sun-dried bricks cemented with bitumen. It was the setting of the story of Pyramus and Thisbe.

l: Pyramus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Pyramus was one of the two lovers in the story of Pyramus and Thisbe. The lovers met near the tomb of Ninus in Babylon, and the tale is presented as a moral story about youthful engagements and parental resentment.

l: Thisbe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Thisbe was one of the two lovers in the story of Pyramus and Thisbe. The story takes place in Babylon and is interpreted as a warning to youth and parents.
